description: Soil to Stars, a team of SWE students using technology to solve problems that matter. we aim to transform NASA Earth data into clear, practical guidance that helps farmers adapt, reduce risk and make smarter decisions. Our name represents our purpose: connecting the soil where our food begins with the stars and satellites that help us build a more resilient and sustainable agricultural future.
summary:
Soil to Stars is a Bangla and English web app that helps farmers in Bangladesh explore how changing weather could affect their crop choices. Farmers select their district and enter their current crop, planting date, and when their field will be ready again. The app connects those answers to NASA POWER temperature and rainfall records and regional BAMIS crop calendars.

For the Field Shift challenge, we built charts that show how temperature and rainfall differed between two decades across all 64 districts. A field report shows the weather recorded during the farmer’s reported crop period when observations are available. The app also walks through a published Bogura field trial, showing how researchers sequenced crops and what weather those crops experienced.

Timing matters when one crop’s harvest determines when the next can be planted. Soil to Stars makes the evidence easier to explore and shows where more local information is needed before recommending a rotation for a specific field.
details:
Soil to Stars is a web app in Bangla and English that helps farmers in Bangladesh explore how changing weather may affect what they grow next. We built it for the Field Shift challenge because the timing of one crop’s harvest can determine whether the next crop fits into the growing season.

Farmers can select any of Bangladesh’s 64 districts or place a pin on the map. They enter their current crop, planting date if known, when the field will be ready again, and their usual growing practices. The app matches the district to a representative NASA POWER weather grid and finds crop calendars for the corresponding Bangladesh Agro-Meteorological Information Service (BAMIS) region. When daily observations cover the reported growing period, the field report shows the highest and lowest temperatures and total rainfall for that period. Monthly and annual charts compare two decades of weather records so farmers can see seasonal differences that annual averages can hide.

We used a published field trial in Bogura to bring crop rotation to life. The app shows the crop sequences first, with planting dates, harvest dates, and historical weather available on demand. We designed the main findings to be readable on a phone and included the original sources so users can check the evidence. Where the trial leaves a date unresolved, the app shows that gap.

We built the interface with Next.js, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and MapLibre. A Python backend processes the weather and crop records, and SQLite stores the data and reports locally. The app calculates results from stored datasets, so generating a report does not require a live NASA request.

Use of AI. We used OpenAI Codex to help build the app, fix bugs, simplify the interface, and test how user inputs affect the report. One prompt asked Codex to check whether changing the district, crop, planting dates, or water access changed the results. The checks confirmed that district, crop, and dates affect the evidence shown. Water access is recorded for future planning. Our team chose the data sources, defined what the app should show, and shaped the farmer experience. The app generates field reports through Python calculations using stored NASA POWER and BAMIS records.

Our goal is to help farmers and agricultural advisers make better informed decisions about planting dates and crop sequences. The current prototype provides historical evidence and a documented rotation example. Recommendations for a specific field require local rules for planting, irrigation, and the time needed to prepare the field between crops.
